This case presents an otherwise healthy adult with acute-onset, non-bizarre auditory hallucinations (negative and command-type) emerging precisely one week after a severe psychosocial stressor — the death of a parent from lung cancer. Brief Psychotic Disorder, With Marked Stressor(s) (DSM-5-TR 298.8) is strongly supported: duration <1 month (7 days), presence of ≥1 psychotic symptom (hallucinations), absence of mood episode meeting full criteria for major depression or mania (despite sadness, insufficient symptom burden for MDD diagnosis), and direct temporal relationship to an identifiable stressor. The hallucinations are the dominant, defining feature — acute, stress-triggered, and isolated — making Brief Psychotic Disorder the most parsimonious and evidence-supported diagnosis.

Brief Psychotic Disorder, With Marked Stressor(s)

While anhedonia was not explicitly confirmed, its absence is not required for this diagnosis; the core diagnostic requirements (1) presence of ≥1 psychotic symptom (hallucinations), (2) duration 1 day–1 month, (3) full return to baseline functioning, (4) exclusion of organic/medical cause, substance, or better-explained mood disorder (e.g., MDD with psychotic features requires mood episode *preceding or concurrent* with psychosis *and* mood symptoms severe enough to meet full episode criteria — here, mood symptoms are present but insufficiently characterized to meet full MDD criteria, and psychosis emerged *after* bereavement *without* prominent neurovegetative changes), and (5) clear association with a marked stressor — are all met.
